title: Verifier‑Grounded Generate‑Verify‑Repair for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Paired Mininet Emulation Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory study (N = 200 intents; 400 paired episodes) to evaluate whether a deterministic verifier‑grounded generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces operationally detectable policy‑violation errors when a hosted LLM produces device configuration sequences from operator intent in a Mininet emulation. Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one sampled initial generation per intent reused by both baseline and guarded). Baseline success (no detected policy violation) = 196/200 (98%); guarded success = 200/200 (100%). Paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.02; preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.125 (primary confirmatory test). An exploratory paired bootstrap (seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples) yields a 95% percentile CI = [0.005, 0.04]. Four verifier‑triggered repairs occurred (total hosted model calls = 204), giving mean extra model calls per intent = 0.02 and mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0. All reported numeric values, provider‑call accounting, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are drawn verbatim from the archived execution and analysis bundle. We interpret the preregistered confirmatory result conservatively and discuss construct, internal, and external validity limits and operational implications.

sections.introduction:
Automating operator intent → device configuration translation is a promising direction for NetOps automation, yet LLMs can produce mechanistically detectable faults—syntax errors, topology/reachability violations, and ACL/policy mistakes—that have operational impact (outages or unintended access) [1], [4]. A common architectural mitigation is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop in which an LLM generates a candidate configuration and a deterministic verifier checks mechanizable constraints; if violations are found the verifier returns localized diagnostics and the pipeline may request a repair from the LLM. Prior prototypes across code and domain‑specific program generation show that verifier‑grounded repair reduces mechanically checkable errors, but open questions remain about scaling GVR across heterogeneous vendor templates and quantifying hosted‑LLM cost per avoided operational violation [2], [3].

This work addresses those gaps with a predeclared, provenance‑traced paired confirmatory experiment executed in Mininet emulation. The study was preregistered as C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 before any model calls and constrained to three synthetic vendor‑template families and four topology patterns (12 strata). Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial sampled generation per intent was produced and reused by both baseline and guarded episodes. Under this design baseline outcome is the validator verdict on that shared initial candidate; the guarded outcome is the final result after deterministic validation and any permitted repair. We therefore evaluate only the effect of deterministic validator/repair actions (not prompt engineering or independent re‑sampling). The manuscript reports only numbers drawn verbatim from the archived execution and analysis artifacts and follows the preregistered analysis plan.
sections.related_work:
Surveys and NetOps‑targeted reviews document rapid growth in LLM‑for‑NetOps research while noting recurring evaluation gaps: provenance, verifier integration, and limited multi‑vendor emulation evidence [5], [6]. Prototype experiments show LLMs can draft network configurations but often introduce syntax, topology, or policy errors; verifier‑guided repair is a recurring mitigation pattern in code and domain program generation [2], [3]. NetConfEval and related tasks provide useful baselines but are task‑limited and often lack provenance‑traced verifier pipelines for audit [4].

Our study builds on these lines by (i) applying a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory design across heterogeneous synthetic vendor templates in an emulator, (ii) executing and documenting shared_initial_candidate semantics so paired differences derive solely from deterministic validator/repair actions, and (iii) recording provider and verifier accounting to quantify repair cost in concrete hosted‑LLM call counts. We avoid claims of production readiness and treat this work as an artifact‑grounded, scope‑bounded evaluation.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment preregistration (C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1) preceded any model calls; its SHA‑256 is 9e0fc992665835975b01289f7841926ef6abf3584252c5d0459ba0ecf166bb50. The primary confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (probability that an intent yields zero operationally detectable violations under guarded minus baseline). The preregistered formal test is an exact McNemar two‑sided test (α = 0.05). Exploratory estimators included a paired bootstrap percentile CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) and descriptive cost metrics (mean extra hosted model calls per intent and mean extra calls per avoided violation).

Sampling, strata, and shared_initial_candidate semantics: N = 200 unique operator intents were deterministically selected and stratified across three vendor‑template families and four topology patterns (12 strata) using a frozen task index profile. Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent exactly one initial sampled generation was produced and reused by both baseline and guarded episodes. The preregistration explicitly declared that independent constrained‑prompt arms were not executed; therefore paired effects can only arise from deterministic validation and any allowed repair.

Model and provider configuration: Archived model configuration declares requested_model = "gpt‑5‑mini" and provider recorded as "openai_responses". The archived model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset; we state explicitly that null/unset is not evidence of deterministic provider sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. Planned generation budget: planned_episode_count = 400, initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_model_calls = 400.

Deterministic verifier and repair policy: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements (i) syntactic parsing and command grammar checks, (ii) required‑command sequencing checks against per‑task required_sequence, (iii) reachability/topology checks using the emulated final state, and (iv) encoded ACL/policy rule checks derived from the task payload constraints. The validator reports validation_before and validation_after traces, violation codes, and a boolean valid verdict under the scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation. The guarded pipeline may request at most one verifier‑triggered repair call per intent; repairs use localized diagnostics from the validator to form repair prompts. Repair calls are permitted only when the validator reports violations. All validator traces and repair decisions are archived per episode.

Scoring, missingness, and analysis protocol: The preregistered primary analysis is the exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary success indicators (no detected policy violation). The preregistration specified conservative handling of ambiguous validator outputs (treat as violation in primary analysis), deterministic duplicate detection (duplicates excluded from primary analysis), and missingness treatments; in execution no pairs were excluded and no episodes failed. The exploratory paired bootstrap CI and cost metrics are reported as descriptive context and labeled exploratory per the preregistration's multiplicity plan.

Deterministic accounting and provider audit: Execution manifest provider audit recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 204 decomposed as 200 shared_initial_generation events and 4 repair calls; cache_hit_count = 0. Stage accounting shows shared_initial_generation = 200 and repair stage = 4. These audited counts are used verbatim in Results to permit independent reconciliation with archived artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution completeness and paired outcomes: The run completed as preregistered: planned_episode_count = 400, completed_episode_count = 400, complete_pair_count = 200, failed_episode_count = 0. The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 196 (both succeed), n10 = 4 (guarded succeed, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (guarded fail, baseline succeed), n00 = 0 (both fail). Baseline success rate = 196/200 = 0.98; guarded success rate = 200/200 = 1.0; paired point estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.02.

Confirmatory test and exploratory interval: The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 0.125 (primary confirmatory result; do not reject at α = 0.05). The archived exploratory paired bootstrap (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) produced a 95% percentile CI for the paired risk difference = [0.005, 0.04]. We emphasize the preregistered McNemar exact test is the formal confirmatory inference and label the bootstrap CI exploratory because resampling intervals can be unstable when the total discordant count (n10 + n01) is small; the artifacts include the bootstrap seed and resample count (analysis_log.jsonl).

Repair counts and cost accounting: Four verifier‑triggered repairs were invoked across the 200 intents. Total hosted model calls = 204 (200 shared initial + 4 repairs), giving mean hosted model calls per intent = 1.02 and mean extra calls per intent due to repairs = 0.02. Because each repair corrected one baseline failure in the archived contingency table, mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0. These arithmetic derivations follow directly from the deterministic_reconciliation and execution_manifest provider accounting.

Representative episodes and validator traces: Representative scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/task‑000004‑*.json, task‑000005‑*.json, task‑000006‑*.json) show identical shared_initial_candidate content reused by both baseline and guarded conditions (shared_initial response files are identical across conditions for each pair). For the four discordant pairs the validator_trace.validation_before recorded the detected violation and the subsequent repair invocation; validator_trace.validation_after recorded repair_applied = true and final valid = true. These per‑episode artifacts substantiate the contingency counts and repair accounting.

Per‑stratum coverage and heterogeneity reporting: The preregistered stratified sampling covered three vendor‑template families and four topology patterns (12 strata) with deterministic assignment prior to model calls. No stratum was excluded; complete_pair_count = 200. Discordant pairs (n10 = 4) occurred in a small subset of strata (per‑stratum discordant counts are available in the archived condition_summary.csv). Given few discordances, stratum‑level exploratory summaries are descriptive only and are reported in the archive rather than used for formal subgroup hypothesis tests.

Statistical power context: The preregistered power plan targeted detection of a 10 percentage point absolute reduction with N ≈ 157; N = 200 was chosen to permit stratified descriptions. The observed baseline failure prevalence (2%) was lower than some planning scenarios, reducing power to detect small absolute improvements and explaining the non‑significant McNemar result despite a positive point estimate. This mismatch between planned sensitivity and observed baseline prevalence is an execution‑grounded reason for cautious interpretation.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation under shared_initial_candidate semantics: Because execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics, each pair began from exactly the same sampled initial candidate; baseline is the validator verdict on that initial candidate, and guarded is the final result after deterministic validation and any allowed repair. Therefore improvements observed in the paired comparison derive solely from deterministic validator/repair actions and not from prompt engineering or different initial model samples. The preregistration explicitly declared that independent constrained‑prompt arms were not executed; readers must not attribute guarded gains to first‑pass prompt changes.

Operational implications and bounded claims: Within the constrained Mininet emulation, synthetic vendor templates, and the validator's encoded rule set, a small repair budget (four repairs) removed the mechanically detectable baseline violations at low model‑call overhead. This artifact‑grounded finding suggests that when a suitable deterministic verifier exists and provides localized, actionable diagnostics, a bounded repair budget can eliminate mechanistically checkable faults for template‑driven emulated workloads. We do not claim generalization to production hardware, other prompt families, different LLMs, or semantic errors outside the validator's rule coverage.

Threats to validity and limitations of inference: Construct validity—the deterministic validator covers syntax, reachability, and encoded ACL/policy checks but cannot detect higher‑order semantic misinterpretations not formalized in its rule set. Internal validity—the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were executed and verified in deterministic_reconciliation, which prevents attributing gains to sampling differences. Conclusion validity—small discordant counts limit power and make resampling intervals less stable; the exact McNemar test is the predeclared confirmatory procedure. External validity—single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), synthetic templates, and Mininet emulation limit claims about production readiness or multi‑model robustness.

Recommendations (artifact‑grounded): (1) Broaden deterministic verifier coverage to encode more semantic/policy ontologies and empirically measure residual false negatives using injection tests; (2) run paired experiments that include independent multi‑sample initial generations per arm to isolate prompt/template effects (not executed here under shared_initial_candidate semantics); (3) evaluate multiple hosted models and model versions to bound sensitivity to provider nondeterminism; (4) preserve provenance tracing for all provider calls and verifier traces to enable external audit. Each recommendation follows directly from observed artifacts and stated limitations.
sections.conclusion:
We preregistered and executed a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory study (N = 200 intents; shared_initial_candidate semantics) that measured whether a deterministic verifier plus bounded repair reduces mechanically detectable policy violations for intent→configuration tasks in a Mininet emulation. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test did not reject at α = 0.05 (p = 0.125). Guarded GVR invoked four repairs and corrected the four observed baseline violations at low model‑call overhead (mean extra calls per intent = 0.02), yielding a paired risk difference estimate of 0.02 and an exploratory paired bootstrap CI = [0.005, 0.04] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000). These artifact‑grounded results indicate that when a deterministic verifier can express and check the relevant constraints and provide localized feedback, a small repair budget can eliminate mechanically detectable policy violations in similar template‑based emulated settings. The results do not establish production readiness, multi‑model generality, or coverage for semantic errors outside the validator. Future preregistered, provenance‑traced evaluations should expand verifier coverage, evaluate multiple hosted models, and compare independent multi‑sample baselines.

References
[1] R. Mondal, A. Tang, R. Beckett, T. Millstein, and G. Varghese, "What do LLMs need to Synthesize Correct Router Configurations?", Proc. ACM, 2023, doi: 10.1145/3626111.3628194.
[2] R. Cadenas, "Convergent Correctness in Stochastic Code Generation: A Generate‑Verify‑Repair Architecture for Deterministic Validation of Autonomous AI Coding Agents in Regulated Environments", SSRN, 2026, doi: 10.2139/ssrn.6754899.
[3] Z. Ding, "Executable but Wrong: Verifier‑Grounded Contracts and Counterexamples for LLM‑Generated Music Programs", 2026, doi: 10.31224/7995.
[4] C. Wang, M. Scazzariello, A. Farshin, S. Ferlin, D. Kostić, and M. Chiesa, "NetConfEval: Can LLMs Facilitate Network Configuration?", Proc. ACM, 2024, doi: 10.1145/3656296.
[5] S. Y. Long et al., "A Survey on Intelligent Network Operations and Performance Optimization Based on Large Language Models", IEEE Commun. Surveys Tut., 2025, doi: 10.1109/comst.2025.3526606.
[6] L. Zhang et al., "A Survey of AIOps in the Era of Large Language Models", Proc. ACM, 2025, doi: 10.1145/3746635.

Preregistration: C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 (SHA‑256 = 9e0fc992665835975b01289f7841926ef6abf3584252c5d0459ba0ecf166bb50) was recorded before any model calls. Sampling semantics: execution used shared_initial_candidate (one sampled initial generation per intent was produced and reused by both baseline and guarded); archived model configuration records temperature = null/unset (null/unset is not evidence of deterministic provider sampling and does not imply temperature = 0). Provider accounting (audited): hosted_model_call_event_count = 204 decomposed as 200 shared initial generations + 4 repair calls. Reported numbers and analysis artifacts are drawn from the archived execution and analysis bundles.
limitations: Scope limited to Mininet‑style emulation with synthetic, provenance‑traced intent→configuration tasks; results do not generalize directly to production hardware or live operations.
Single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) evaluated; multi‑model generality is not established.

Deterministic validator coverage limited to mechanically checkable errors (syntax, reachability, ACL/policy encodings); higher‑level semantic or specification misinterpretations outside the validator may remain undetected.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics imply observed paired differences derive only from verifier‑triggered repair; this design does not measure effects of alternative prompting strategies or independent multi‑sample candidate selection.

Observed confirmatory effect (2 percentage points) did not reach statistical significance at α = 0.05 for N = 200 (exact McNemar p = 0.125); low baseline failure prevalence (2%) reduced power to detect small absolute improvements under some preregistered scenarios.
